Children of the Sun is described as a "puzzle-shooter", but the experience reminds me more of the first phase of infiltrating a base in a stealth-action game. Each level sees you circling around a location, tagging enemies, noting patrol paths, and observing environmental hazards that can be used for extra damage.

Once you take the first (and only) shot, Children of the sun reveals its main mechanic - telepathically guiding the bullet.  Sometimes everything will go according to plan, but even if it doesn't, you can often improvise a solution 'mid shot'. This mix of planning, timing, and thinking on the fly is incredibly satisfying.

The level design is great throughout. New mechanics are introduced every so often, and each level has a different focus. Some are tight spaces with more obstacles, some are more spread out, some focus on enemy movement, etc. Aesthetically, the levels echo a variety of dingy, real-world locations where one might expect cult members to be hanging out.

The presentation is excellent. Art style is exactly what you would expect from a game published by Devolver: lo-fi assets, stylised violence, and surreal environments. The music has a similar vibe, contras

Definitely worth the full asking price, but if you see it on sale, GRAB IT IMMEDIATELY. This game deserves all the love.

Neon White: Sniper Elite

Scout an area, plan how you're going to take out everyone, screw up, improvise, try again, and come up with new ideas for improvement. 

The core Hitman gameplay loop, boiled down to a 30-second speedrush of you flying a bullet to its destination, paired with the joy of competing with your friends' scores, is the most easy to pick and play pure fun coming out of a sniper rifle I've seen.

With a 3-4 hour story mode, and another 1-2 hours to finish up the optional challenges that each level has, it's wonderfully paced and very respectful of your time. If you want more you can come back and compete with your friends on the leaderboards for hours on end. 

Lovingly crafted, interesting aesthetic, great pacing and a nice take on storytelling. This one has it all.

Children of the Sun is a puzzle shooter stripped down to just the core puzzles and the aesthetic. The style is very minimalist and psychedelic, the plot is barely there and follows the jumbled chronology of your protagonist's crumbling mind, the levels themselves contain lots of "errors" that quickly become too obvious and drastic to be anything but either magical or psychosis on the part of the protagonist.

And it works! The puzzles are what's on display here and they're good. Everything else works towards communicating how broken the protagonist is. The puzzles are truly unique and very satisfying... and the plot communicates a story about how our need for control damages the people around us. There's so little here but everything works because they put the thought into making sure it was put together excellently.

And the price! It's so cheap! Well worth the cost of entry. If you want shorter games with worse graphics made by people who are paid more to work less and you're not kidding... this is a game for you.

A genuinely fascinating and original game, loads of fun to figure out and execute the levels, and I want to put it on my wall and my stereo. Strong recommend.

There is a pretty basic revenge story to follow as you play the game, but it’s told in a very stylized way with very little dialogue and it covers some pretty dark themes. It’s mostly told with flashes of 2D comic panels that have a really cool graffiti art style to them. The environments are pretty great for the most part though. Everything is dark, dingy, and surreal; and the soundtrack compliments it very well. But the OS,OK method is not just a medal to be awarded on a flick in a multiplayer lobby here: the one bullet in your gun is your one opportunity to slay all your enemies in front of you.  You must kill them all in order to maintain your secrecy and continue your mission.  But how do you kill multiple people in different places with one bullet fast enough to avoid alerts?  Telepathy.  Telepathy and a lot of Hate.

You are THE GIRL, fighting a past plagued with atrocities and trauma brought through THE CULT that she joined and was raised in, is out to kill THE LEADER, a mysterious long haired aviator-donning man who set THE GIRL on her path to vengeance. review_text_for_llm:
I. Am. Obsessed. Children of the Sun is a terrific puzzler, just dripping in the most heinous of vibes. I had high hopes for this game's sniper mechanics, and I am glad to say those hopes were surpassed.

It starts out relatively simple: try to find the right out to shoot a handful of guys. I will say, it was during this phase that I wondered if this game really had meat on the bone, or if it was just a cool premise with evocative art.

After the first few missions though, the puzzles began to evolve at a thrilling rate. The number of missions I ended breathlessly triumphant over clever geometry and mechanics make me positively giddy.

There is also, like, WAY more content than I expected? I went into the game knowing that it was about 4 hours long, but those 4 hours are just so DENSE with fun. The missions don't take long, there are a ton of them, and not a single one feels perfunctory.

Basically: This game is TIGHT and pristinely polished. It's a game where you can feel the developers' fascination with their own premise, and the result is sublime.

[h1]One-shot, A Bunch of Kills[/h1]

Puzzles and shooting games don't usually go hand in hand naturally, but Children of the Sun has somehow stuck the landing. Constantly testing your patience and problem-solving skills, one bullet is all you have, it's also all you ever need.

I loved the visuals above all else in this game. The gameplay is a lot of fun and challenging (if you care a lot about high scores) but it does sometimes lack a certain polish in terms of the bullet's hitbox. Overall, the game is rather short, if I did not care for scores or achievements, I'd likely finish it within two hours or less. The price is something to be desired as well unless you're the type to be on the top of every leaderboard in each level, you may wait for a worthwhile sale.

Even if I won't play Children of the Sun again anytime soon, my four hours experiencing this visual treat was more than I could ask for.

review_text_for_llm:
A visually arresting sniper/puzzle game where you telekinetically control a single bullet that you use to kill members of the cult you escaped from. Every time you hit an enemy, you can redirect the bullet from that point, so it's initially all about figuring out the order to kill them so that you can continue to play connect the dots with your targets, but it eventually layers on more powers for you and more challenges to overcome in enemy types. 

It's so aggressively styled in every aspect of it, from the eerily colorful visuals to the unsettling soundscape to the frankly kind of edgelord story beats (the game was originally pitched as "I Just Killed a Man and Now I'm Horny" so that can kind of give you the vibe it's going for). It's all so singular and of a piece that it just feels like a such a complete package. I beat it in 3.5 hours, and it felt like they got about all they could out of the mechanics presented. Some of the puzzles were thrilling, requiring quite a bit of timing and precision to pull off.

It's definitely not for everyone (stylistically, thematically, or gameplaywise), but I loved it. Laser focused in every aspect to communicate a ver specific vibe.

review_text_for_llm: I really dig "Children of the Sun". You play a masked sniper - whose look reminded me somewhat of the movie "The Crow" - on a mission to wipe out some kind of religious group. The details are hazy, as the plot is presented through a bunch of confusing cartoons. That's fine though. We've learned from "Hotline Miami" that context is not a necessary pre-requisite, but a seasoning. "Children of the Sun", unlike "Hotline Miami" is not a franticly-paced action game. It's a strange kind of puzzle piece, where you guide one single bullet from enemy to enemy, sometimes bending time and space to land a perfect head shot. Through a liberal use of slow motion, it gives you ample time to consider your next move. The catch is that you have to nail all the enemies with one bullet, and the bullet can't touch anything that doesn't bleed or explode, or it's game over. Is that sort of ridiculous? Oh yes. Is it great gameplay? Duh! "Children of the Sun" does its premise justice, and fully delivers on the potential of its central gimmick. Its grungy aesthetics, noise-filled soundtrack and ridiculously violent gameplay hit just the right spot for me.

At the core,  this is a puzzle game about spotting all targets, plotting a trajectory and finding the right timing to take your shot. 

The game introduces new mechanics quickly and wastes no time adding more layers to each puzzle.
-->Playing with mouse is recommended for precision, it is a sniping game after all.
-->A keyboard is entirely unecessery for Children of the Sun.
-->Playing on steam deck is possible, but joystick controls make precision more difficult.

You can beat the game in 4-6 hours, allthough the challenges and leaderboards may give you additional playtime.
It's a short, but great experience that makes you wish for a bit more.

review_text_for_llm: Absolutely nails the grindhouse aesthetic and story even if the storytelling is very fast paced with blink-and-miss glimpses of flashbacks to understand Girl's motivation to kill a cult leader. The story ending has a nice dark twist, and in general was reminiscent of Midsommar at times. It's very accessible too, just needing the mouse as you move from left to right on a plane to deliver the killing shot that will dart from target to target, and you can leverage blowing up the gas caps on cars or birds in the sky to get better positions. The progression in enemy types pairs well with the abilities you develop like slow-mo, redirecting your bullet, and kaleidoscopic weak spots on enemies. A nice feature is once you've tagged the enemies, their positions stay even if you fail, which means you're not wasting time and can focus on optimising the route for your bullet. Overall, there's a certain dark and vengeful mood this hits along with the killer girl grindhouse aesthetic that makes for an engaging sniper puzzle shooter that doesn't lose steam by the end.

[h1]Criminally Short, Satisfyingly Sweet[/h1]

[h1]Things I Like About Children of the Sun:[/h1]

[b]1. Sniping puzzle game. Carefully observes the stage, marks your enemies, shoots, and guides the bullet through every skull.[/b]

[b]2. Every stage has a little challenge for bonus points and another layer of puzzle. Players can deduce the context via the short message below each stage's title.[/b]

[b]3. Although there are only three abilities introduced, each of them adds a surprising amount of depth in your sniping route.[/b]

[h1]Thing I Like And Dislike About Children of the Sun:[/h1]

[b]Short Playtime[/b]
A dilemma as old as time. A short playtime means the gameplay is compact, showcasing all the interesting elements to the fullest before everything loses its novelty. Then again, a short playtime also leaves the player wanting, craving for more satisfying headshots and more interesting stage puzzles.

review_text_for_llm:
A short but sweet puzzle-shooter game where you brutally kill everyone with one bullet, bouncing from head to head. The presentation is amazing, with the animated cutscenes being gritty and loud, making for this intentionally disorienting feel. 

Gameplay is very punchy, with your one bullet having the impact of a freight train. You have to connect the dots between everyone on the map, flying your bullet from person to person. While there are some routes that are obviously better than others, CotS gives the opportunity to return to previous levels and try different routes, and maybe increase your score on the global leaderboard. Later on in the game, where you unlock more ways to manuever your bullet, it only adds to the punchiness. Definitely enjoy <3

Audio works well. While the music isn't nothing super standout, the sound effects is where this game also shines. You FEEL the sound of the bullet whizzing through the air, picking up speed. You FEEL the impact as you shatter some random dude's kneecaps.

Recommend from me <3

This game has a lot really cool aspects that make for a really unique experience.  
Attributed to the story, it come off as intense or heavy but in actuality, its a really nice and chill puzzle game with that dopamine hit you get from sniper play. 

This can be work friendly game because it is fundamentally a casual puzzler you can play on mute BUT to really get you money's worth, I think you wanna play with sound.  Not that the music is good or anything, it's just that sound really adds to the experience. 

Its fun that the game changes things up by adding pac-man, fishing, and car chaser mini games.  Surprising and fun for a game that feels really linear. 

It's also super stylish, with retro PS2 graphics.  Something about the cut scenes really remind me of twisted metal 2's which is really enjoyable and keeps you looking forward to them.

The cult story is fun...and very adult... but its non-linear reveal keeps you engaged. 

BTW fun story: there was a family that lived across the street from me growing up that had been part of a cult.  The father had to chase down the cult in Europe and rescue his 1st wife and her/their(?) son.  He was successful in the rescue and they all live

[I]Children of the Sun[/I] is a unique and fun puzzle game about a girl getting revenge on a cult with a sniper rifle and powers that allow her to kill 20 people with a single bullet. From a gameplay perspective, once you shoot, you are playing as the bullet (and it's casing, which I assume is the result of a European developer lol). It has a very unique and unsettling art style, which combined with the music creates a really compelling atmosphere for the game.

There are many different ways to kill all the enemies in a level, but there are specific challenges on most levels that require you do at least one specific thing, usually prompted by a vague sort of riddle that is fun to figure out.

The game is not too long, it took me about 4 hours to beat. I recommend it for anyone who likes puzzle games and doesn't mind violence.

review_text_for_llm:
This game is a masterpiece of an indie game. It is more of a puzzle game than an action game (considering this game can be played with one hand), so there will be lots of trial and error and thinking. But it also allows you to yolo once you master the mechanics and are more comfortable with them.

It's concept is pretty unique. Although it does remind me a lot of SUPERHOT (which I also really enjoyed).

Everything is just right about this game. The "puzzles" aren't too hard. The dialogue is minimal (thank god). I loved the cutscenes and the story! The game's length is perfect for the price. The difficulty is perfect. The achievements are perfect (you can easily 100% them if you try).

The "intermission" missions are interesting, fun, and a nice welcome break from the normal bullet puzzle missions.

They style, artwork, title of the game, and mission names/phrases are amazing and very well done.

The tutorials are short and sweet and nicely integrated.

Basically nothing in this game overstays its welcome.

Perfect, bite sized game! High recommended.

Historians should study this game as a lesson on how to design a game properly.

Children of the Sun takes the usual bullet time effect, where a camera follows the bullet until the point of impact and flips it on its head by letting you control the bullet itself.

The game gives you both new abilities and interesting new enemy types throughout its short 3~ish hour run, each one of these pretty drastically changing your approach to certain missions.

I hope that the developers patch in both a level designer / editor, and an option / gamemode that allows the player to visit previous levels with their newly unlocked abilities to potentially give the game a bit more longevity, because currently I wouldn't say that the 15€ price point is entirely justified.

Here's what the gaming industry is meant to be all about, developers trying to be innovative and different! And even though Children of the Sun might not have longevity, it sure has captured my imagination.

If you look closely to the visuals you'll see that the graphics are pretty basic all round, but that is overshadowed by the psychedelic art design. Everything from the colours, lighting, sound and definitely the story projects a surreal atmosphere that, even though might not be for everyone, sure is original. But not as original as the game play. The mechanics of moving around and shooting people with a sniper rifle are simple, but the overall premise plays more like a puzzle game. You have to really think and plan each move before stringing together that one 'magic bullet' shot. I did start to find the process a bit tedious after a few levels, but this will definitely appeal to perfectionists out there, as there plenty of avenues to tackle each level.

Whether you are a fan or not, games like this deserve praise for originality. And since the price is so cheap, especially when its on sale, it is well worth giving it a go.

My only issue is the sound design, a few times it can be very grating on the ears. There is also level "X" which blasts you with sudden flashing colours and I was not ready for that! 
I feel for $15 if you know what you are getting it's worth it. But I would recommend finding that under $10 deal for a good "I really got my money worth" feel. I did 100% it in 4 hours, but used a guide to help understand each levels clue. If you decide to go in blind, some of those clues may be difficult to figure out and prolong that play time to a fair bit. 
Don't over look this, it set out to do something and it pulled it off well!

Cool Game! I think the presentation is really what sells this title for me. At its core its a simple premise, you are a sharpshooter and you get to control the trajectory of the bullet after getting a kill. The more you play the more complicated the levels become and the more variety of enemies the game introduces. Every Map acts as a puzzle that you have to solve which are pretty open-ended with the solutions (for most maps) with things scattered across for you to use. The story is pretty weird but after a few cut-scenes, you understand what is going on. The game can get a bit repetitive after a few hours though, as not a lot changes, only what I stated (New enemies, Harder maps). They do introduce new abilities after a few levels, but it's nothing that changes the gameplay drastically, just more to aid you. 

Seriously though the presentation really sells this game. It's weird but gritty. Bright and colorful, but Dark and Foul. Brandish but Abstract. It's so unique that I would say for that alone you should try the game out. It's damn fun with a personality that stands out on its own.

A neat little indie game where you're a supernatural sniper taking down an abusive cult that she was a part of before (born into) and escaped after they killed her parents

Since her powers are to shoot one bullet and guide it from one kill to another, the game is essentially level-based snooker puzzles, with each shot needing to go further and in more complex ways to beat the level

Enemies gradually ramp up from unarmoured, to riot shields, to full body armour - requiring different skills that unlock in the level progression to take down

Most levels have an additional challenge given to you through a cryptic clue at the menu, some are more challenging than others - the singular Steam guide available was helpful for me to pick up the specific requirements for a couple, but for the most part I could intuit the challenge from the clue

The story is given through drawn cut-scenes and a few special levels that integrate the game mechanics - reasonably well done in terms of making a hate-able antagonist and reason for the violence

review_text_for_llm:
First off, I love Children of the Sun alot. I don't feel as though I see the comparison enough but it has the soul of Hotline Miami, stylistically and especially if you hunt for high scores. Levels are short (<1 minute generally) and retries are nearly instant, so if you make a mistake the turnaround is super-quick (outside of one level with a 45 second timer you can choose to wait for to get a higher score). Levels are also very constant. Enemies move predictably based on what you do, so it makes it easier to perfect your path through the levels. This also results in it being much more of a puzzle than a shooter; you have to plan your route carefully to make sure that by killing one enemy, it doesn't make it impossible for you to reach another. Wrapping back to my earlier comparison to Hotline Miami, this is what made me love both of them (HM and CotS): methodical planning followed by a frenetic, high energy execution.

The time to beat CotS is probably about 3 hours if you are choosing to go for raw completion (no challenges, high scores, etc.) but if you want to try to optimize routes and get better at each level, it will probably be closer to 6-8 hours.

This might just be my platonic ideal indie game. Simple controls meet high-concept gameplay, with outstanding art direction reminiscent of movies like Mandy (2018). More of a score-attack puzzle game than a shooter, the campaign tasks you with efficiently clearing out cultist filled environments using only a single, telekinetically-controled rifle bullet. Pacing is tight, with a steady drip of new gameplay wrinkles to keep things interesting, and an ending that arrives well before things start to get stale. Plus there is a new hoard mode for anyone worried that the story might be too short.

If I were to nitpick, there are some problems with the UI. I accidentally reset all my progress at one point, but it didn't take long to catch back up. Otherwise, if the gameplay footage looks even remotely up your alley, Children of the Sun is a must play.

review_text_for_llm:
Phenomenal art direction. No notes.

The gameplay's core concept is rather basic, but well-executed: you have one bullet to kill a bunch of enemies, but as long as you manage to take down an enemy, you get to fire another shot from the bullet's last position. As you keep advancing, both extra abilities and complications are introduced, keeping things sufficiently varied.

The total number of levels isn't all that high, which is both a blessing and a curse: the game doesn't last long, but I fear it'd be extremely likely to overstay its welcome if it had more content to offer, because I feel there's only so much you can extract from the game's concept.

The difficulty is largely on point. It gradually rises over time, but never becomes overbearing; the final level might be an exception here, with its two phases being a touch obnoxious to deal with, but it's a minor misstep at worst.

Overall, Children of the Sun is a perfectly fine distraction for an evening or two. I would love to experience more of the same in terms of art style and the setting (it's painted in broad strokes, but the gist alone is potent enough), but as for the gameplay, I've had my fill.

This is a lot to like about Children of the Sun. The art direction is impeccable, the story is compelling, and the first few levels promise a really creative gameplay experience. However…I don’t think the game lives up to the hype of the first few levels. 

For the first half (or maybe two thirds) of the game, there are a number of ways to complete each level. It’s fun figuring out the different ways to kill everyone with a single bullet. But as they introduce more and more enemies that can only be targeted through specific means, they cut down on player freedom. There is eventually one real solution for each level. And it becomes less fun once it turns into a game of guess and check rather than creativity and strategizing.

Do you wish Far Cry 5 was a puzzle game about the Magic Bullet that killed JFK? If so, Children of the Sun might be for you!

Children of the Sun is a 3D trajectory puzzle game where you are a girl who fled a 70s cult. In each level, you have one magic bullet to kill a bunch of cultists. Each time your bullet hits a target (including wildlife or explosive devices), it stops in place and allows you to reaim and fire it again. The challenge lies in plotting a route that provides vantage points on each cultist at the right time. 

Of course, Children of the Sun has some other tricks up its sleeve as well. You unlock the ability to curve or even redirect your bullet in mid-air. The enemies get abilities and upgrades as well to ensure the learning curve stays fresh. 

Level design is a huge highlight. Children of the Sun was a short, relatively fun game for its runtime. I found it most interesting to view it as an exercise in game design. It's basically the simplistic art of drawing a straight line in 3D space, from one target to the other. Its simple gameplay loop is both the most interesting thing about it, and also a slight detriment by the end. There are a few changes that cause gameplay to deviate as you get farther into the levels, but nothing that really changes the core experience. It's a puzzle game at it's most base layer. How to move an object from A - B - C, using snipers and purples colors to express that.  

From an artistic and aesthetic point of view, it's unique. I enjoyed the style, but the music and story were nothing to write home about. The music never moves beyond a humming drone, and the story was something I completely ignored. 

Overall I'd recommend it. If you're the type who likes indie games that do things out of the box, you'll get a kick out of it. Its maybe 4-ish hours if you rush through, 6.5 if you do the extra achievements.

review_text_for_llm:
Children of the Sun is puzzle-shooter game in which you manipulate a single bullet in specific ways to kill cultists. 

This game was surprisingly difficult towards the end! I was kind of breezing through the earlier levels as I imagine is generally expected, but the last four or five levels probably took me 20+ minutes each to figure out. Of note, I was completing each level’s challenge as I went, so it might be slightly easier if you skip those, though not by much. The game introduces a few mechanics throughout that hinder/grant abilities, which is what primarily led to the increase in difficulty.

In general, I really enjoyed the art design, the narrative that's shown (in an edgy/dystopian sort of way), and the stylized nature of the game. The puzzles were fun and interesting, and I haven't seen another game like this so it was truly unique (to me, anyways) in its juxtaposition of two genres. 

The game took me 6.5 hours to complete and I thoroughly enjoyed my time with it. If you enjoy puzzles, cool art design, and/or are looking for something a little different, then this game is easy to recommend. 

Edit: Updated to unmissable given how much I still think about this game lol.

[H1] Children of the Sun is a mood [/H1]

Whether you like puzzle games with a little extra flair or got edginess to your core (like I do) you will enjoy this. 
Very little story to speak of but what is there is told brilliantly through little comics and dream sequences all with that edgy dream like neon aesthetic I absolutely adore. It doesn't matter that it's not all explained, the game sets the mood for killing cultists perfectly.

The premise is very simple. It's Sniper Elite, puzzle edition. You have to figure out in what order to kill the enemies using the tools provided. From the moment you shoot you are the bullet and you can take as much time as you want to pick your next target (in most cases). As the game progresses you unlock a couple more powers for your bullet.
That's it, it's a glorified but satisfying connect the dots game but coupled with the visuals it elevates it to a unique enough experience to be worthy of your time. 

That is... if it was cheaper (or you grab it on a sale). The price is way too expensive for what this game offers. It's 25 missions and it's more of a big long tutorial rather than the game pushing its mechanics to its limits.

review_text_for_llm:
Children of the Sun is an experiment combining the critical thinking of a puzzle game with the satisfaction of shooting someone in the head.

You play a telepathic sniper, bouncing your single shot from target to target. Occasionally using your abilities to curve the bullet, like in my favorite James McAvoy film, Wanted.

Most levels follow a simple formula. An open area, a staggering of cultists who require bullets in their brains, and a plan to maneuver a single shot through them all. As the game progresses the enemies will protect themselves, gaining bulletproof shields or heavy armor that requires an extra heavy shot. Some will be on patrol, making timing the moving target a priority. And then other levels break the formula entirely. There is a whole car-chase shoot-out sequence that is just fantastic. Suffice to say the game never gets boring, it always has a reason for what it's doing.

The narrative is very straightforward, letting the environment and character design tell the real story, with occasional flashes of voiceless memories to drive it home. The sound design is solid and the visuals are stylish. It all combines to a slick presentation that is just oh so satisfying

I played the demo of 'Children of the Sun" way back and finally played through it recently. What a tight little puzzle game, boiling over with grungy neon style! Despite looking like killer7, CotS plays less like a rail shooter and more like Katana Zero meets frisbee golf. The only looming threat is FAILURE to weave your one bullet through every cultist in the level. The dynamic soundtrack shouldn't distract from your focus: Prowl the outskirts with a crawling bass, then send your bullet flying to a psych-guitar crescendo!
Ricocheting from head to head with a bullet's POV is exactly the catharsis I needed when I downloaded this game. 
  The story took me around 5h total with a few breaks and a lot of hitting my head against the wall (not out of difficulty per se, but because the later levels demand more finesse, and benefit from trial-and-error). I think I'll circle back to The Girl's revenge odyssey when that singular mood strikes next. In the meantime, the wave shooter mode might be an interesting way to kill time (but I'm never getting close to the score of user 75,000 waffles!).
My favorite map was probably the Open Mic Night in Hell. What I assume was a JPEGMAFIA reference

[i]Children of the Sun[/i] is a sniper-puzzle game; each level you get one shot to take everyone out, but have the ability to slightly control the path of your bullet in flight, and get to re-launch the shot after every successfully hit target. Levels are quite creative, and new elements are consistently introduced, including new abilities for you to use, more challenging enemies, and more complex environments. Each level also has a cryptic challenge for you to solve. 

The game is incredibly stylish, it's got this eternal sunset color palette, psychedelic cartoon scenes, and a lifeless cold environment. It contributes to an eerie atmosphere backed by this dark droning soundtrack. Each level has leaderboards as well, giving it a score battle element that I know I would've had a great time with if any of my friends had times posted. Finding the best solution is only half the battle, execution of the strategy requires semi-precise inputs, and good timing. I thoroughly enjoyed my time with [i]Children of the Sun[/i], and went out of my way to do everything it had to offer. It's an easy recommendation if the above sounds interesting. 

[b]Recommended[/b]

Children of the Sun is essentially a puzzle game about killing your way through a cult with one bullet. Each time you hit a target, time stops and you get to reaim and shoot at another one.

The levels start out easy aim-click-reaim-click, but as the game goes on, more and more complications are added to the missions. You'll unlock the ability to curve bullets, reaim midflight (limited per 2 critical hits) and speed up the bullet to hit through armoured enemies. Some of the later levels took quite a bit of trying to figure out the best path to hitting everyone.

The art style is really cool, reminds me of grindhouse horror movies, which does seem to be like one of the inspirations.

You get scored on your runs, so there is some replayability there. In addition, there is an endless mode, but I have to be honest, coming off of the hand designed levels it feels bland and barren.

My only complaint is that the game is very short - around 3 hours with retries. Not necessarily a bad thing, just something to keep in mind when deciding whether to buy the game full-price or not.

Recommended!

The sequel is out, and while I know there's a lot of comments along the lines of "it's more of the same but better", I want to try to talk about how the game is generally different and how that works to both the game' advantage and detriment.

So let's talk about those changes and how I feel about them.

1. Rather than have a space-based inventory management system, you now have a weight-based one.  While your guns and the ammo in them don't count towards it, everything you stuff into your pouch does.  You do get upgrades to boost your weight capacity (by essentially just stuffing balloons into the bag to make it lighter).  Items can overlap though, making it hard to tell how much ammo or what healing supplies you have left though, meaning you periodically will have to run maintenance if you want things to be neat and orderly for those frantic moments.

2. Levels are generally larger, more sprawling, and non-linear  Your goal with each level is to find the terminal that unlocks the elevator clearance that lets you go to the next floor. Fun and complex where it counts, the new crafting system adds a depth to the inventory system that the previous game lacked while the continuation of the story is spot-on where it has to be. Alternating periods of excess where you have more resources than you know what to do with and scarcity where you're worried whether or not you have enough ammo and healing for your next encounter are exactly what I like seeing in the survival horror genre, and this title manages that rollercoaster beautifully.

My only complaint would be the final boss. On normal difficulty, it feels as though it has a bit too much health unless you're hitting its frustratingly elusive weak spot, drawing the fight out immensely. Combined with the fact that the game's very premise makes it easy to get caught menuing at a bad time, and it can make for a frustrating experience.

Beyond that one single encounter at the very end of the game, this is a significant improvement over the original, which was already an interesting and entertaining game. Everything from the movement to how your inventory works pairs well with the ominous narrative to make for a fascinating experience.

Unfortunately not as good as the first game. If you haven't played it already, get that one instead.

All of the fun, frantic, one-handed gameplay from the first one seems watered down and somehow more clunky. A few examples:
-You no longer remove the empty casings from each slot of the revolver and replace each one, instead you just drag all the bullets into a single slot and then they're automatically emptied when you fire.
-Scrolling to open your inventory is replaced with a physical bag attached to your torso that you have to reach for, which is often hidden under your body or your gun, making it annoying to open.
-The map is now on your watch, so you open it by clicking with your hand in front of your face. I usually enjoy when a game mechanic is a physical object in the game world like that, but in this case it means you're probably going to accidentally open the map whenever you try to interact with something that's in front of your face.

The worst change, though, is the introduction of a crafting system. In the first game, you just find bullets and syringes; in this one, you find pens and nitrocellulose which you use to craft bullets, weak syringes and nitroglycerin

I'm a big fan of Endoparasitic and while the sequel improves on some stuff, I can't recommend it because of a couple of major issues.

[olist]
[*]The new [b]inventory system is a MAJOR QoL downgrade[/b] imo. Scroll up for inventory was perfect, but the new system of dragging a bag behind you is terrible. Sometimes you end up with the bag under you and you can't quite click to access it.
But [b]the worst issue is if you get jumped by an enemy and go to quickly grab a gun, but misclick on your bag - you end up sitting there in your inventory whilst the enemy attacks you and it is absolutely infuriating[/b]. 
This problem is massively amplified by the introduction of these new challenge sequences where the enemies can move really quickly. In these cases, you have a fraction of a second to react between an enemy entering your field of vision and attacking you, so you do need to snap aim to get your gun out; misclicks are inevitable and the game punishes you for it in the most frustrating way here.
Then to close, you now have to click a button in the top right, which is way slower than the old scrolling down system; so if you do misclick on the bag, you're guaranteed to have a bad time.

As someone who played and thoroughly enjoyed EndoParasitic 1, it pains me to say that this was an absolute letdown. I’ve never been more disappointed in a sequel than this. That being said the game isn’t terrible by any means, it ran very well and the gameplay itself is pretty much the same as the first game, which is fine. But everything outside of that just left me feeling like this was a massive step backwards.

1: The game has a MASSIVE focus on crafting. Now let me be clear when I say that the crafting system isn’t bad at all, that’s not what I have a problem with. What I do have a problem with is how the game basically forces crafting on you. The only items that you will ever find while scavenging is nothing but crafting materials, you will never find anything pre-made for you. ( With the exception of the times the game introduces you to those items, the game will give you some ammo to start with when you get the handgun or the shotgun for example. ) 

I know the benefit of having a crafting system like this is that it allows the player to pretty much choose what resources they want, but at the same time I thought this made the game a little too easy with resource management.

This game is great, and I recommend it, but here are some of my constructive criticisms:

1. Melee needs a major buff. When I first booted up the game and was comparing the weapons between characters, I saw a melee sword had the same base damage as a wand and a bow. The fact that melee weapons deal the same damage as ranged and magic weapons is not great design, there needs to be a trade off for being, y'know, in melee range. Time and time again game developers don't give any innate advantage to being a melee class when there is the obvious disadvantage of being a melee class.

2. Weapon Power needs to be scaled on an attribute similar to Spell Power. I personally love playing primary attack builds and there is no way to get WP anywhere near as strong as SP. Maybe WP on Dex/Strength, SP on Int/Focus or something along those lines.

3. Most items just aren't that exciting. Because of the ARPG-style gear, a lot of the strength and joy of picking up the roguelite loot (trinkets) has been toned down. Also, the ARPG-style loot could use for some more variety as well. Would be cool to see Epic or Legendary/Unique tier of loot with special effects and more affixes (maybe even set bonuses)

Meta progress doesn't reset, but run progress does, so each time you restart it you're more powerful, but you go through the same low level areas at the start.  This gets boring, but you can't skip the areas because there are powerups you need to collect.  The designers seemed to know this and put in a way to skip the first boss once you defeat it the first time and it gives you all the powerups you would have missed having not gone through that part again.  Either I completely missed that they did that for the rest of the bosses or they just didn't do it.

Very early review, but:

Positives:

- Great pixel art.
- Nice soundtrack.
- Cool minor voice acting from the p/c.
- Hits (you deal) feel chunky.
- Nice build variations with random drops.

Negatives:

- Some mobs will just spawn on top of your head, surround and kill you with no prior indication, ending a promising run.
- Unavoidable traps (tripwires in singular corridors) which force-pull huge groups.
- Rocks falling from the ceiling that dumpster your HP mid-combat. There's no indication of these. The game expects you to be running around/strafing constantly, apparently.
- Levels are very long, and death sets you very far back. Not just a couple checkpoints. You have to do everything all over again.
- Feels unbalanced. Doesn't feel tight.
- 100% gives me eyestrain, the constantly moving textures blending together is a real eyesore/hits the motion sickness aspect pretty badly.

I'm not feeling the £15-20 price-tag on this. Might refund before I enter the sunken cost fallacy

The maps and enemies are always the same, and the upgrades you find during the run ("trinkets") are almost always just small stat boosts. There are shortcuts after having completed certain bosses in the initial playthrough for each difficulty (new game +1, +2, +3,...,+n), but the shortcuts are designed so badly that you are missing on essential upgrades for your character which is ultimately leading to death in the later stages of your run wasting hours of your time.

Speaking about wasting hours, the developers are not respecting their players time.

review_text_for_llm:
It's not fun anymore after about 250 hours.
The game has an NG+ system (a.k.a endless mode) that gradually reduces the player's defense as they progress. However, that doesn't cover up the fact that the game has very little content. The character classes and builds are unbalanced. This leads to players being forced into a fixed build, which only exacerbates the problem.
And the solution they came up with was to buff the monsters to be stronger and harder to kill. The normal monsters are even more annoying than the bosses. All of this is to slow down the player's progress. However, that goes against the purpose of NG+ mode, which is to make the monsters naturally stronger over time (because the player's defense decreases while the monsters' power increases).
Then they rework and tweak it a bit. Sometimes things that were working fine are tweaked to an imbalance that ruins the player's experience. it makes me feel like this isn't even a finished game, just a poor early access release.

*Dashing is a thing now.

This game has all of the bones for something great, but really boils down to mindless grinding through enemies that die instantly until you get to a point where you die instantly, then repeat, getting slightly further every time. There are dodgeable projectiles but often times there will be so many projectiles or such a dense fog of damaging AOE that you can't dodge it due to the very slow movement speed and very slow regen of dodges.

Itemization is boring, just simple stat increases - more mana regen, more dex, more int, etc.

It's possible that with a fully upgraded and leveled character in NG+ the game is more fun, but there isn't anything to test those characters against anyways, just the same old couple floors with the same old enemies.

Unless it gets a lot more content and a proper random roguelike mode, I can't recommend the game. But it's not horrible either, so there is some fun to be had if you're looking for a short 5-10 hour distraction.

The potential of the game turns into frustration and disappointment of what could be a fun game that is simply not fun the more you get into the game.

I really like the meta progression ideas of the game. I like how they give so many ways to upgrade your player power whether that is through upgrading your characters stats, leveling up other characters for account wide buffs, upgrading trinkets, finding new buffs / recipes, upgrading your town, etc. The game has so many systems that you feel like you are always progressing to something, which is a key element to a rougelite. Initially these systems made me think that I would put in a ton of time into the game (100 of hours) before getting tired of the content. However, that wasn't the case. 

The issues arise once you beat your first run. You start to realize that the game has really poor balancing issues and those mechanics to increase player power are really just bloat,  as a lot of those mechanics become useless at a certain point.

I played the demo a while back, and with how the game was released, I'm very disappointed. 

If you liked the first game, this is very similar to it now, which is why I'm writing this review. In the demo version I played, the game was much more of an exploration game; there were plans to make it so players could create their own "stories" that followed a narrative and whatnot (as an additional thing to the base game). The player base apparently didn't like the fact that HOH2 was not going to be the first game again, so they complained. 

Now, the devs decided to do what the vocal side of their audience said (fair), but they reused a lot of assets to make the first game within a slightly new system. A lot of mechanics that felt like arbitrary grinds returned, the "tax" system (now a forced "donation", thankfully you don't have to use lifts to send stuff back, but now your materials are taxed as well), the town building, that's all they feel like, forced grind to slow the game progression down. I don't like it as a sequel to Heroes of Hammerwatch. This plays like a diablo spinoff, which by itself is fine, but i'm comparing the two games to each other.

I don't like the UI. The first game's UI felt better, and for some reason this game doesn't seem to improve upon the problems of the first game's UI. There's still no minimap, there's only a toggleable map which covers the whole screen. The player UI feels worse than the first game's, especially when it comes to cooldowns and experience.

In the first game, Everything you kept on your character was something you purchased in town as a passive upgrade. There was not a direct equipment system. I never played hammerwatch 2, which might be where the equipment system came from, and it definitely seems more dynamic in this game, but this isn't what I was expecting to get from this game at all.

If you're into diablo like games, this game isn't necessarily bad by any means, at least for what I played of it, but if you're expecting a game that feels like heroes of hammerwatch 1, and you haven't played through it's DLCs yet (like me), just grab the dlcs instead, cause maybe we'll have more fun with it.

Really enjoyed the game as a simple little ARPG
Probably my favourite aspect is the town building, it feels like each run I was progressing to something
The general curve of unlocking new power also correlated quite well with getting a bit further each run, making it a satisfying grind
That being said I feel the game can become quite monotone over time running what feels like the same zones with almost no real build choice. The trinkets offer a great way to make runs more interesting, but being so limited with each class makes it a bit monotone imo.
Another great feature is being able to switch characters, yet once you spend most of your ressources into one, it makes playing other classes a bit more painful cause you feel like losing so much of your progress.

Overall I'd say give the game a shot if you enjoy ARPGs, you can get a good 10-15 hours worth of fun gameplay and perhaps even more if you want to try out more different things.

I really wanted to like this, but after playing it some more, I just get irritated.

Is it worth the price? Sure. But don't think that this is ANYTHING like the first game.

Here's why:

1. I beat this game within 10 hours. I think it was about 40 hours for the first one. Bosses were actually hard in the first game and you had to learn their moves. I just stand still most of the time and do very little active playing. Nothing from skill or learning the fights.
2. Very little variety between runs. Very small pool of trinkets (per-run equipment) and 75% of the time I get the same exact sets. Just check out the wiki for the first game which has a HUGE pool of items that made runs varied.

I'm very conflicted about this game. I've been waiting for the successor to HoH1 for years now. Hammerwatch 2 came out, i bought it, disliked it and uninstalled it very quickly as it was not the experience i was looking for. 

HoH2 finally releases and i'm ecstatic. The first 15-20 hours were like a blast from the past and very enjoyable, but as you play the game you come to realize that the game has regressed to a worse state of what HoH1 was in terms of gameplay, progression etc.

A lot of things are reused from their previous games and its just a headscratcher. If they can reuse 70% of enemies, items etc why don't they add all the mechanics and things that made their first game so beloved? The game is also plagued with endless amounts of bugs.

I cannot recommend this game as of right now to anyone who's played HoH1, and are looking for a similar experience, as its just a straight downgrade from the first one unfortunately. The game doesn't feel polished or finished. This doesn't feel like a full release, but rather an early access state.

However if you're new to the franchise i can give it a pass, but i'd still recommend playing Heroes of Hammerwatch 1 instead of this.

Promising But Needs More Polish 
This roguelike shows potential but currently feels underdeveloped in several key areas. The procedural generation needs work, as levels tend to look too similar across runs, reducing that sense of discovery the genre thrives on. Build variety is limited right now, with many talents not providing meaningful choices - some, like the 'chance for extra 45 fire damage,' don't scale well into late game, and certain high-level abilities (such as level 155 Rogue spells) can feel weaker than basic attacks.

The progression system has some rough edges too. With a level cap in place, hitting a wall at max level means your only options are to either level other characters or hope for better gear drops to improve your stats.

There's definitely a fun core here, but it needs more environmental variety, better talent balancing, and more satisfying progression systems to reach its full potential. Keep an eye on updates if you're interested, but right now the game doesn't quite deliver the depth and variety that roguelike fans expect.

review_text_for_llm:
Just like the original Hammerwatch had to crawl so that Heroes of Hammerwatch could fly, it seems history repeats itself here. 

While the story-driven Hammerwatch II had tons of issues that never ended up being solved, some of its improvements over the original like the graphics and inventory system have carried over to the rogue-like spinoff beautifully. The equipment system creates a better feeling of improvement over each run and the gear can be shared across all your characters. Gradually building up your town between runs, seeing it prosper with more and more people walking around is really satisfying as well.

In essence, this game is like Rogue Legacy and Gauntlet had a baby. It took me a few hours to get into it, the first area (Forest) isn't as fun as the cramped hallways filled with secret areas of the subsequent zones. But once you get pretty far into your runs, all the good vibes from the first HoH come rushing back.

Do you like ARPGS? Check

This game is a blast if you dig high intensity dungeon crawls with your friends(or solo). The game acts like a traditional rogue-lite, where you pick up new abilities and trinkets that disappear after the run. But there is another layer of diablo style equipment that persists through runs making every run feel meaningful. Additionally, you have a huge town upgrade system that allows you to use the various currencies you accrue in a match to give you permanent buffs to your character. Combat is fast, frenetic, and fun. When playing solo, death means your run is over, in co-op, you can resurrect your friend at a cost of a penalty to the max HP of you and your friend for the rest of your run. 1 death is no big deal, even 2 or 3, but the more times you die, the higher likelihood you will both wipe out in a hairy encounter.

A fun game. I love how much there is in the form of the hub building over time.

TLDR; Don't buy it if you plan on playing it on Steam Deck until some big loading improvements are patched in.

One *major* negative for anyone who wants to play this on the Steam Deck: The loading times are *very* poor. Setting graphic settings to the lowest doesn't change this ONE BIT. I only play single player so it's not network speed either.
My best guess is that this game tries to load every single sprite of the entire map separately. Even once you're in the map, it's frozen for a minute, then it lags a LOT until at some point it freezes, after which the speed is mostly fine for the first few maps. Later on you're playing at under 10 fps.

I really hope this gets addressed.

I never played HoH 1, so this game was fresh for me. Initially, I enjoyed it quite a bit, but replayability is shockingly low for a game billed as "rouguelite." I got all classes to NG+, but it's just too much of a repetitive grind to proceed from there.

Every run's progression of enemies and stages is exactly the same. You always face the same enemies in any given level, bunched into the same groups. Bosses and boss stages are precisely the same every time, occurring in exactly the same position in the sequence. The only thing different about any given run is the - relatively narrowly randomized - layout of the stage. However, because stage layout has no impact upon strategies used in fights, it's a cosmetic difference and each run feels exactly the same as the last.

The game is relatively cheap, but it's not worth the money. I have 45 hours of play time, but I enjoyed maybe  15 of them. The rest is me (far too slowly) coming to grips with the fact that I just cannot do this.

I wish there was a neutral option for this game – because for almost all intents and purposes, it’s an improvement over the predecessor. To start with the good, it’s gorgeous, the doing away with keys and soul linking is fantastic, multiplayer is far more seamless, extra types of resources feels better than I would have expected (i.e. wood, stone, iron, etc.), and the boss fights are all pretty great.

The issue I have with it though is an identity one almost? In the first game, if you start a new save, you will die within a reasonable time getting sent back to town to upgrade and get further next time, as is how roguelites go. Making mistakes felt really punishing in the first game – if you get yourself into a bad spot, you will feel it. Traps are brutal early on; enemy density can be quite high and getting cornered is very dangerous. This game doesn’t seem to have that. I like the graphics and gameplay but the progression design in this game renders it an exercise in utter tedium. Right at the start you need  to run through 2 fairly large forest levels and 2 even larger dungeon levels. This takes about 20 mins. Then you fight the boss, and if you die (and you will, a lot), you lose much of the haul you had gathered and then have to do it ALL OVER AGAIN. 

Add to that bullet sponge enemies that are a bore to fight and the ability to heal yourself only TWICE in total per run and you end up spending 60% or more of your time in this game sitting doing nothing in a quiet corner of the map waiting for your health and mana to recharge so you can progress. That recharge takes 2+ minutes.

Easily the most tedious and dull game I've ever played. And I didn't even mention the random boulders that can fall on you any time and anywhere and will one-shot you. Even when you are examining loot on the ground from the chest you just opened. Crush!!! Random boulder.

Do I heck.

For masochists only.

The best part of the game is the charming pixel graphics. The way the wind blows through the trees as you walk is such a pleasant touch, and the overall pixel retro vibe is what initially drew me into this game. I haven't played HoH 1 so I can't compare. 

Once the nostalgia wore off, the mediocrity became very apparent. The character builds don't have any variety beyond "damage number go up", and the music is somewhat bland. I can kinda see the appeal with the base building element, but after an hour or two of playing, I couldn't bring myself to enjoy or care about anything else on offer. If you're wanting a dynamic home base feeling in a game, play Hades. For a variety of classes and builds, play Halls of Torment. Both offer much more interesting gameplay loops.

While the gameplay is enjoyable and I've enjoyed my time playing, I do have several major gripes about the game that I don't think patches can correct.

- Buildcraft is basically nonexistent. You want to pick up every trinket every run for the most part. Even if the trinket doesn't benefit you, there are several other trinkets that scale your character per trinket owned making getting every item every time mandatory. 
- Class specializations boil down to (mostly) the same things and there isn't much variety in playstyle, and some of the more interesting specializations are numerically bad and fall off, forcing you into a handful of specs if you like to play in the higher NG+ levels. 
- Trinkets cannot be stacked, so there are no "builds" really. You just take what you get and most runs you will end up with 90% of every trinket in the game by the end of each run, making it extremely shallow and rather repetitive after clearing the first several NG+. Lots of build diversity with the subclasses and ability upgrades you can find on runs, some classes have more build variety than others (Warlock, Paladin, and Rogue in particular I find to have the fewest options). Lots of ways to make progress, both on the character and savefile level.

Its a bit grindy but the grind at least feels fun. Every aspect of the game has ways to mitigate the grind, such as global bonuses to all characters and ways to upgrade and choose the modifiers for your gear. The most egregious part is definitely the blueprint grind to max out your tavern, enchanting, and trinket attuning options but all of those are linked to your savefile not your characters.

Devs have done good on updating the game post launch to add and adjust content to be the best it can. Probably among the best games of its kind right now.

There are a bunch of people talking about movement making them feel nauseous and forced mouse acceleration but I don't think they have realized its actually just raw input delay. I'm also aware of the Chapel Building that reduces the death tax, but this is not sufficient in my opinion. The tax just feels bad. There are some interesting concepts with this game. Unlike games like Diablo or PoE, where creating a new character restarts the world from scratch, Hammerwatch has interplay between all characters. As you go through each level, you collect resources which allow you to create buildings in your little township. Each of these buildings serves a different function. Shopping, upgrading weapons and armor, etc.
Any character you create will automatically have access to the town buildings that you've unlocked. Each character you level up adds bonuses for all other characters, such as increased HP, armor, or attack. This is a nice touch, because at least you don't feel like you're wasting your time by trying out different characters. 

But that is where the fun stops with Hammerwatch 2. This game is an absolute grind for the sake of grind. You will run the same dungeons over, and over, and over again, as you try to level your characters and your town.

review_text_for_llm:
I'm nearing 50 hours and I have enjoyed playing each character on the first playthrough. The spells are cool, the classes feel distinct (especially after level 10), and the rougelite aspects, such as trinket attuning, give some nice "power up" feeling to the game.

However the game quickly stagnates after the first playthrough. Enemies get much stronger, with the increases to player power (with the exception of a class or two) lagging far behind. In addition, the town building feature ends quite abruptly and then that's it, your resources are then meant to alter runs (make them a little easier). You could make the point that the developers are trying to work this out (as seen in the frequent patches made to the game), but then what did I buy? Many who have reviewed the game already are critical of the "bare-bones" feeling. As if this is an early access product as opposed to a completed game and I have to agree. 

This is an okay game in its current state with the potential to be absolutely fantastic. For now, I would recommend wish-listing and monitoring its progress in the coming months.

When the game first came out and all the players were of a low level it was extremely fun, one of the best drop-in multiplayer games I've ever played. 
But then within a few weeks everyone was higher level and at higher level the game changes from a tense but fast paced dungeon crawler with deeply required teamwork and roleplay (combat wise) into; everyone is a flourescent pink flashing anime character with lasers shooting out of their orifices in every direction and tearing across the map by themselves at the speed of light obliterating hordes of enemies and in an instant breaking the setting, the atmosphere and the gameplay.
If the developers could capture the essence of that early game experience, perhaps cap player movement speed harder (and naturally slow down enemies/missiles etc in turn) and remove the pink powerup laser system I think they would be most of the way to making the game what it could be. But as it stands I'm not interested.

review_text_for_llm:
The best 80s/90s action RPG you'll play each time you play it. The characters are fun and different. The pixel art is compelling and sometimes difficult to parse visually but in a way that makes me feel nostalgic for my childhood games rather than frustrated. The meta progression is confusing in a similar way, purposely vague and with little to no explicit tutorial. 

My only complaint through my first few hours before I sat down to write this was that for a roguelike/lite the runs can be very very long. If one thinks about the game as an RPG first and a roguelike second, then the pacing is more appropriate. The character swapping one might do in a game like Isaac doesn't feel quite the same here. Each character has it's own individual progression and in the course of a run will occasionally find gear or unlocks that benefit a different class, compelling you to jump into that one and maybe even getting excited at the idea of dying on your current character so that you can jump back onto the wizard.

I would certainly purchase this for the sale price of $20 and I think that for $40 you won't be disappointed. It is a vast improvement over the original and a unique gem.

As a huge fan of the original Heroes of Hammerwatch, I was incredibly excited to hear they announced a sequel, and Heroes of Hammerwatch 2 absolutely delivers!  It takes what made the first game one of the best roguelike experiences out there and builds upon it in meaningful ways.

While it's true that it doesn't have the sheer volume of content that its predecessor boasts yet (give it time, it just launched!), the new features and refinements are fantastic. The gameplay feels incredibly smooth, and the retro-style graphics are as charming and effective as ever. The core game loop is addictive and rewarding, constantly pushing you to explore further and conquer new challenges. It's clear the developers have poured their passion into this project.

If you were a fan of the original, or if you're looking for a top-notch roguelike with a great sense of progression and satisfying combat, look no further. Heroes of Hammerwatch 2 is a worthy successor and a fantastic game in its own right. I'm incredibly excited to see what the future holds for this game and can't wait for any future DLC! Highly recommended!

This is an early access game masquerading as a full launch. It's a decent rogue-lite with an insanely shallow gameplay loop. While the town building is fun and leveling classes to 20 is an ok experience, there just isn't enough content to justify a ~$20 price tag. There are still insane balance issues, and the game definitely needs to add a lot more gear/items/trinkets/upgrades to make the NG+ grind feel worthwhile. 

It's also been over a month and we still have yet to see anything added besides a few minor tweaks and bug fixes. I'd suggest waiting at least 6 months to a year before giving this a go. It has a potential, but right now, not enough to make it worthwhile.

Edit: It's now 9 months since launch with zero additional content added besides bug fixes and balancing. Unfortunately, this game is not worth $18 in its current state and the devs refuse to explain what actual content they will add, if any, and whether or not it will be free or paid DLC. Negative:

You can clearly see that the Devs put love into this one.
Haven't come across any bugs during my playtime.
Nonetheless, I cannot recommend it for personal reasons.

I didn't like the music, this is the first game I ever played where I turned the music to 0.
The ambient sounds from attacks as well as monsters become annoying quickly as well.
The combat is pretty slow paced, at least early in the game. This might increase when unlocking more upgrades but it's too slow for my liking so far.

During your runs you'll find passives that might increase your dmg, armor, life, mana, etc. There are a lot of choices that spice up your spells/skills as well. I liked this aspect so far. These passives will all be gone after every run.
The equipment you find will be carried over. Sadly, I didn't come across any decent equipment, so for me the 3 runs I did so far all felt the same. And it wasn't particularly fun either just blasting the same 2-3 spells at enemies in every corner.
I wish I liked the gameplay more cause I am curious to what the base-building aspect has to offer, but I just can't push myself to try another run which I know will be 95% the same to the last 3 runs.
But like I said, me

Game was amazing at the start, no issues at all. Great game play. Gameplay is still great. I'm not sure if there's a save file issue or something. But what I can tell you is after NG+1 my friend and I playing online coop will have our games lock up. Locking up to the point where we have to force close and restart the game.

Sometimes it will be his game only, sometimes its my game, sometimes its both. I run Fedora, he runs Windows 11. Single player causes no lock ups, but the moment we group together its a matter of time. We are not the only ones reporting this issue as there's been a couple people reporting the same issue on discord. 

I think the biggest disappointment is the lack of support from the developer. Both of us have sent in crash logs for the game via email and their discord support channel. All 4 reports have yet to have any response from developers. Not even a "We are looking into it". These were sent 2-3 weeks ago now.

Great game, bad support, game from a coop level is borked and I can't recommend.

Ever thought doing laundry could be fun? Well, Laundry Store Simulator tries its best to convince you it can be. With a quirky concept, minigames to keep you busy, and a progression system that lets you turn a dingy laundromat into a washing wonderland, there’s definitely potential here. But much like a mismatched sock, not everything fits perfectly.

[b]Graphics: 5/10[/b]
Let’s be honest: the visuals look like they were borrowed from a mid-2000s game. It’s not ugly, but it’s definitely not winning any beauty contests either. The machines, laundromat interiors, and customer designs are all functional but lack the polish that would make the game more immersive. If you’re here for eye candy, you’re in the wrong spin cycle.

[b]Gameplay: 6/10[/b]
The concept of running a laundromat is surprisingly fun, and the inclusion of minigames adds a nice twist. Sorting clothes, cleaning machines, and tackling quirky challenges keep things engaging—at least for a while. The grind, however, can get tedious. This is another shop-like sim game which is actually entertaining enough to keep playing. It is not a difficult game, and it has the typical shop sim game mechanics poured into a laundry business. 

Is it a perfect game? No! It is an early access game, like many other current shop sims out there. It has some bugs and gameplay can be obstructed because of it. So far, I have had a very fun gameplay without many issues. 
If you like shop simulation games, this one will probably be fun for you too.

So, the core business of the game is to upgrade your laundry business. Grind money for upgrades by doing the typical chores in the shop. You do laundry! 
You start off with the cheapest machines, a washer and dryer, which break down regularly. The first three machines are not that expensive. After I got 6 washers and 6 dryers, the cheapest kind, I quickly upgraded to the second-tier machines, which cost 26 bucks per machine. I managed to use these machines until my shop reached level 3. 

There are more expensive machines, which I haven’t used because I didn’t feel the need for it. I guess that the breaking down mechanic will be reduced with higher tier machines. Maybe the time gets reduced

This is a really good game, but there are a few things I'd like to see fixed as the game grows:
1. The restocking employee, should prioritize stock that is the lowest (not restocking a soda every time someone buys one).
2. There should be some type of stock breakdown on the empty wall of the storage room. It would tell how much of each item you have in the storage room, so you don't have to go looking in every box to see what you're running low on (a computer would work too, plus you could adjust the prices of everything from the computer if a second one was put in the storage room)
3. The employees that wash/dry should also have their priorities tweaked a little. There have been many times where a ton of dryers were done and the iron/folding employees were just sitting around because they weren't being brought any baskets.
4. I don't always receive notifications when certain NPCs are heading toward my store (vomiters, smokers, graffiti, etc). Sometimes I don't know that they're coming until they've already done something to ruin my the tips I should be receiving.

Aside from those things, I think this game is something special! And I really look forward to watching it grow!

Surprisingly Addictive — Laundry Store Simulator is the Chill Grind I Never Knew I Needed

As someone who usually leans toward action RPGs and competitive shooters, I didn’t expect much going into Laundry Store Simulator. I figured it would be a fun little distraction — but 20 hours later, I’m fully invested in building the ultimate laundromat empire.

First off, the gameplay loop is surprisingly satisfying. You start with a rundown laundry shop, barely making enough to keep the lights on. But as you upgrade machines, optimise workflow, and add little quality-of-life improvements (like vending machines and better decor), you start to see the place come to life — and your profits soar. Watching those quarters pile up is weirdly thrilling.

The pacing is great. The devs clearly understand the dopamine hit of incremental progress. You’re constantly unlocking new features or equipment, and the upgrades actually feel meaningful. I especially love how you can automate parts of the business once you’ve built up enough — it scratches that management-sim itch in the best way.

Visually, it’s got a clean and cozy vibe. Nothing too flashy, but it fits the chill, low-stress atmosphere.

As you progress, you're able to install coin-operated machines, open a mini-mart, offer custom T-shirt printing, and optimize delivery logistics. ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ 510/10 – The Dark Souls of Laundry

Laundry Store Simulator is not a game — it’s a lifestyle. One moment you’re upgrading your washers, the next you’re playing janitor, bouncer, and therapist all at once.

Machines constantly break down, and the only fix is to smack them with your trusty wrench. If you don’t, puddles appear, and customers wipe out like it’s slapstick comedy hour. Meanwhile, NPCs keep turning your bathroom into a smoke-filled vomit lounge, kids graffiti your walls, and some random squatter uses your work computer to stream videos.

Customers aren’t normal either. Some just leave socks in the machines, some climb into the washers themselves. When that happens, the game gives you two options: “Help Customer” like a professional, or “Help With Love,” which spawns pink hearts everywhere like you just proposed to someone stuck in a spin cycle. Romantic, right?

Oh, and did I mention the clowns? Because apparently, half the town moonlights as circus rejects. Add in the occasional guy who walks in wearing nothing but underwear, and suddenly your laundromat feels less like a business and more like a fever dream.

Yet through all this chaos, you still feel proud.

The game doesn’t introduce anything new, but it’s competent enough to satisfy a typical simulator craving.

Simulator players generally fall into three categories: story focused, standard, and min/max players. This game alienates min/max players by turning the tutorial into a rigid set of mandatory steps required for progression.

Laundry Store Simulator genuinely surprised me. After putting about 10 hours into it, I can confidently say this isn’t just another shallow simulator built around a single gimmick. Running a laundry store is only the foundation—on top of that, you can manage self-service coin machines, handle delivery orders, create custom shirts, operate a mini-market for supplies, and even set up vending machines for extra income. It constantly feels like there’s something new to unlock or optimize, and juggling all these systems never feels overwhelming thanks to how well they’re introduced over time.

What really stands out is how thoughtfully the progression is designed. Skill upgrades, store expansions, and new services all feed into one another in a way that feels deliberate and rewarding. Hiring employees, improving efficiency, and unlocking new features creates a steady sense of accomplishment rather than artificial grind. Every upgrade feels meaningful, and the game does a great job of encouraging you to reinvest earnings instead of hoarding cash with no clear purpose.

I also love the personality layered throughout the experience. Random side quests, recurring NPCs, and quirky characters

There's more recipes, relics, parts and maps to explore, but the rest is either just like or very similar to the first game. This also, unfortunately, means the minion AI hasn't really been improved at all. You still have the option to manually control a selected minion, but outside of that there's only basic commands like "get resources" or "fight enemy bases" and that's all. The AI can feel frustratingly stupid sometimes, but maybe that's just because you're controlling undead dudes you cobbled together with glitter glue.

It's still fun for me though. It's not perfect, but it definitely scratches that tower defense itch. I also enjoy the bits of humor throughout.

This game is very much like the first, with some changes. If you liked the first Necrosmith, you will most likely enjoy the second game as well.

Necrosmith is a really fun and addictive game about building minions with multiple body parts and sending them to fight and loot for you. You can give them basic orders and personally control one of them at a time. There is also the possibility to build very strong but costly special units called titans.

In each run you have access to some offensive, defensive and utility spells and can also find upgrades that provide different bonuses for your units and tower or additional body parts. 

After each run you can spend the gold you earn in permanent upgrades for your spells or base body part generation. There is also a “relic” system that allows you to select up to four modifiers/bonuses.

It’s a very enjoyable small game.

- Building your minions is very fun
- The art is awesome
- The attack animations are cool
Cons:
- Extremely unpolished, feels like a very early access
- Controls are wonky
- AI is stupid (EDIT an update has since come out improving the AI, they're still not perfect but it is much better now and is no longer a major issue)
- Missing many important quality of life features such as selecting groups of minons, giving specific orders without needing to micromanage, etc.
One of my biggest gripes is that the game provides practically zero information on the DPS of weapons... there's a flat damage number but nothing telling you attack speed, range, AOE etc. Impossible to create good builds without tedious trial and error.
At the end of the day it is a $10 game, but the developer just didn't implement so many easy improvements that would have dramatically increased the quality of the game, so I cannot recommend it in its current state.

For games like this that are roguelites, I tend to be a completionist so there's much more to do after completing the story line. There are many relics to be found and upgrades to be made. My typical relics are- rollerskates, Frankenstein's head, pocket magnet, and holy grail. Spoilers- +50% movement for controlled dead, +1000 hp for dead created from 3 different races, circle radius for controlled dead for resource pickups, and +250 gold +50 ore +50 mana for destroyed lairs. Swapped out Frankenstein's head for chaos gem (+3000 gold for killing a boss).
It's a great game for the price.

Having said this negative stuff: these are really just ideas for the developer and not pertinent complaints. I loved this game and would gladly pay for more content like this or for this. I'm only throwing stuff out there because, well, vested-interest. There's barely any games like this on the market, so I'm inclined and incentivised to provide anything that'd make this game better than it already is, or for future products similar to this.  

Great game, strongly recommend if you loved Majesty or any similar GodGame Strategy titles.

Okay, played for three hours, feel ready to write a review.
Short and sweet, I am enjoying myself.

Developed and published by Alawar, the sequel once again places you in the enigmatic role of a necromancer who commands a magically infused tower in the middle of a hostile, procedurally generated world. Your mission remains deceptively simple: survive waves of enemies, explore the surrounding biomes, gather resources, and steadily grow your undead legion.
